title: IBBI Lets a Committee of Creditors Hive Off One Stressed Real Estate Project From a Builder's Insolvency
meta_description: IBBI's Fifth Amendment lets a 66% creditor vote carve one stressed project out of a developer's insolvency, with separate project bank accounts.
court: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
case_name: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) (Fifth Amendment) Regulations, 2026
citation: IBBI/2026-27/GN/REG155 dated 30 October 2026; Press Release IBBI/PR/2026/18 dated 31 October 2026
body: Any resolution professional who has run a builder's insolvency knows the problem. A single corporate debtor often holds six or seven separate housing projects, and the moment one of them lands in litigation or stalls for want of clearances, every other project under that same company gets dragged through the same resolution timeline, whether or not it had anything wrong with it. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India has now given committees of creditors a formal way out of that trap. On 30 October 2026 it notified the Fifth Amendment to the CIRP Regulations, 2016, which lets a stressed real estate project be carved out of a multi-project developer's corporate insolvency resolution process without restarting the insolvency for the company as a whole.

The mechanism sits in a new set of disclosure and voting steps. At the very first meeting of the committee of creditors, the resolution professional must now place project-wise information on the table: each project's RERA registration, its construction stage, the number of units already handed over, and the claims still pending from allottees who have not received possession. Once that picture is in front of the committee, it may recommend exclusion of a specific project from the resolution process, but only with at least 66 per cent of the voting share, and only with reasons recorded in that recommendation. The final word still belongs to the National Company Law Tribunal as Adjudicating Authority, which has to approve the exclusion before it takes effect.

Money is the other half of the amendment, and arguably the more overdue half. Each real estate project under a corporate debtor must now be run through its own bank account, with the resolution professional reporting project-wise receipts and payments to the committee instead of one consolidated figure for the whole company. That closes a gap that resolution professionals have quietly worked around for years: collections from allottees of a nearly finished tower being shown as available to settle claims tied to an entirely different, stalled project under the same corporate shell. The Regulations now tie fund use directly to the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, so money collected for a project has to be spent on that project.

Resolution plans for these companies will also look different going forward. A plan now has to deal with homebuyer claims project by project, stating whether a buyer gets possession, a refund, or a transfer of the allotment, along with a stated timeline for finishing construction. A companion circular issued alongside the amendment tells resolution professionals to put up CIRP notices physically at the project site within seven days of their appointment, rather than treat an upload on the IBBI website as sufficient notice to people living near, or waiting on, the project. The same circular asks resolution professionals to keep meeting RERA's disclosure obligations through the resolution process rather than treating the Code as having displaced them.

None of this addresses an imaginary problem. Homebuyers who paid for a flat in one tower of a project have routinely found their own possession held up by a dispute over a different tower, or a different project altogether, purely because both sat inside one corporate debtor's CIRP. Resolution professionals had no regulatory peg to separate the two even where doing so was the obviously sensible course, and committees of creditors, lacking a rule to point to, often chose not to improvise. The Fifth Amendment gives both sides a framework they did not have before.

The change took effect from the date of its publication in the Official Gazette, so resolution professionals already running a real estate CIRP will need project-wise disclosures ready for their next committee meeting rather than their next quarterly report. For a homebuyer stuck in a largely complete project of an otherwise troubled developer, the practical consequence is that possession no longer has to wait on an unrelated project clearing its own insolvency, provided the committee of creditors can muster the 66 per cent vote the Regulations now require before the Tribunal will even consider the exclusion.
why_it_matters: Multi-project developers are common in Indian real estate insolvency, and bundling unrelated projects into one CIRP has delayed possession for buyers with no stake in a sister project's troubles. The amendment gives committees of creditors a 66%-vote route to separate projects, forces project-wise bank accounts, and ties resolution plans and fund use to RERA, changing how resolution professionals must structure a real estate CIRP from their very first creditors' meeting onward.
card_summary: IBBI's Fifth Amendment to the CIRP Regulations lets a 66% creditor vote exclude one stressed real estate project from a builder's insolvency, with project-wise bank accounts and RERA-linked resolution plans.
card_tip: Developers and resolution professionals handling multi-project CIRPs should prepare project-wise RERA, completion and claims data before the first committee of creditors meeting after 30 October 2026.
verification_notes: Notification date (30 Oct 2026) and press release date (31 Oct 2026) confirmed by Taxscan, TaxGuru and LiveLawBiz. The 66% voting threshold for project exclusion and the Adjudicating Authority's role confirmed by Taxscan and LiveLawBiz. Separate bank accounts and RERA-linked fund use confirmed by TaxGuru and LiveLawBiz. The site-notice circular (CIRP notices displayed within seven days) confirmed by LiveLawBiz; TaxGuru covers it as part of the same package. Monitoring committee composition and exact quorum/voting rules for that committee were not confirmed in any source and are omitted. The regulation number (IBBI/2026-27/GN/REG155) comes from a third-party regulation tracker (CrackTarget) and is reported with that caveat.
